items.title: 20-year buy-and-hold portfolio backtest: $100K becomes $399K, beats S&P and ACWI by not blinking
items.idea: Blind Squirrel Macro backtested a hypothetical 'Mosaic Portfolio' built for a 20-year hold: $100K grew to $399K, compounding at just below 7.2% annually, despite a full 10-year drawdown from 2008 to 2018. It beat a naive 'Extrapolation Portfolio' by 8.6x while also beating the S&P and MSCI ACWI.
items.angle: The individual stock picks are still paywalled, but the real signal isn't the names — it's that a strategy which stomached a decade-long drawdown without being touched still compounded through it and crushed both benchmarks and the naive-momentum alternative.
items.tweetA: A 20-year backtest just showed a portfolio beating the S&P and MSCI ACWI while surviving a literal 10-year drawdown (2008-2018) without being touched. The lesson isn't the CAGR, it's that 'boring and untouched' beat 'smart and active' by 8.6x.
items.tweetB: 8.6x. That's the gap between a stock-picking framework built for 20-year horizons and one built by naive extrapolation. Most portfolios today are optimized for the next earnings call, not the next two decades.

charts.desc: No chart in the plain-text email — podcast/newsletter hybrid, screening tables are paywalled.

items.title: Global EPS estimates are breaking their usual seasonal pattern — upward, not down
items.idea: 2026/27 EPS estimates for the MSCI All Countries World index are rising against the typical sideways-to-down trajectory seen through the year, and the share of countries seeing negative YoY earnings revisions has dropped to cycle lows.
items.angle: Breadth of upgrades, not just US mega-cap earnings, is doing the heavy lifting for the global bull case — but downgrade breadth dropping toward zero and turning back up is historically a contrarian top signal, and there's no sign of that turn yet.
items.tweetA: Global earnings revisions almost always drift down through the year. This year they're going up. That's the actual bull case for equities right now, not AI capex headlines.
items.tweetB: Downgrade breadth at cycle lows sounds bullish until you remember it's also the setup for the next downgrade cycle. The signal to watch isn't the level, it's the turn.

charts.desc: MSCI ACWI 2026/27 EPS estimate revisions chart (via @MikeZaccardi).

items.title: Tech insiders are buying into a 3-month stall
items.idea: US tech stocks peaked in early June and have been range-bound since, but corporate insider buying has picked up pace during the consolidation — a classic 'insiders know something the tape doesn't' signal.
items.angle: Insider buying during a flat consolidation is a different signal than insider buying during a drawdown — it reads as conviction the stall is temporary, not a value trap.
items.tweetA: Tech has gone nowhere for 3 months. Insiders are buying anyway. That combination — flat price, rising insider conviction — has historically preceded a resumption of trend more than it's preceded a breakdown.
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching NVDA earnings Wednesday for the AI verdict. Meanwhile insiders across tech have already been quietly voting with their own capital during the stall.

items.title: Record short futures positioning in the Nasdaq — by the 'smart money'
items.idea: Asset managers and hedge funds are running record short futures positioning in the Nasdaq even as insider buying picks up in the underlying names — a direct contradiction between two 'smart money' cohorts.
items.angle: When institutional futures positioning and corporate insiders disagree this hard, it's usually fuel for a squeeze in one direction — the question is which side blinks first into Jackson Hole and Nvidia earnings.
items.tweetA: Hedge funds are running record short Nasdaq futures. Tech insiders are buying the underlying stock. One of these two 'smart money' cohorts is about to be very wrong, and NVDA earnings Wednesday might be the tell.
items.tweetB: Record short futures positioning isn't bearish information, it's squeeze fuel. Combine it with heavy S&P short interest and you've got two separate mechanisms primed to force buying, not selling.

charts.desc: Asset manager / hedge fund short futures positioning in Nasdaq (via @MacroCharts).

items.title: S&P 500 short interest is 'a LOT of bearish positioning sitting underneath a bull market'
items.idea: Schaeffer's flags heavy total short interest across S&P 500 components even as the index sits near record highs — meaning there's substantial latent buying power if shorts are forced to cover.
items.angle: Combined with the record Nasdaq futures short data, this points to a market where the bear case is already positioned rather than building — which changes the asymmetry of a rally versus a selloff into year-end.
items.tweetA: The S&P is near highs and short interest is still heavy underneath it. That's not a market waiting to crack, that's a market with a coiled spring under it if the bears are wrong.
items.tweetB: Positioning data this week tells two different stories depending which desk you sit on: bulls see record short interest as dry powder, bears see it as smart money front-running a correction. Both can't be right, only one gets paid.

items.title: India has underperformed EM by 44.9% — the worst gap since 1996
items.idea: India's stock market has lagged the broader EM index by 44.9%, the worst relative underperformance since 1996, as investors price India's outsourcing-heavy economy as an AI disruption casualty while Taiwan/Korea chip stocks lift the rest of the EM index.
items.angle: This is a pure 'AI winners vs losers' trade dressed up as a country allocation call — the real question is whether markets have over-extrapolated AI's threat to Indian IT services, which would make this one of the cleaner EM contrarian setups going.
items.tweetA: India vs EM: worst relative underperformance since 1996. Not an India-specific crisis — it's Taiwan and Korea chip stocks pulling EM up while India's outsourcing economy gets priced as AI roadkill. That's a very specific bet to be making 44.9% wide.
items.tweetB: Every AI-loser trade eventually gets a re-test of 'did the market overreact.' India's IT services didn't suddenly become worthless because AI copilots exist — but the price already assumes something close to that.

charts.desc: India vs MSCI EM relative performance since 1996 — a straight line down (via @JeffWeniger).

items.title: VIX is sitting on the floor right before Jackson Hole
items.idea: The VIX is bouncing along the bottom of its range, and seasonality points toward a volatility flare-up around now — candidates for the trigger include Fed hike odds, rising bond yields, Jackson Hole, or Middle East/midterm/Europe geopolitics.
items.angle: Low vol is a better predictor of future high vol than of continued calm — stacked against this week's calendar (NVDA, PCE, Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech as Fed chair), the setup for a vol event looks unusually loaded.
items.tweetA: VIX floor plus Jackson Hole plus NVDA earnings plus PCE, all in the same week. If you're short vol into this calendar, you're not being contrarian, you're picking up nickels in front of a very specific steamroller.
items.tweetB: Nobody knows what triggers the next vol spike, that's the point of vol. But 'low vol right now' plus 'four major catalysts this week' is as good a setup as seasonality gets.

items.title: Top 10 stocks' forward PE just fell to the bottom of the decade's range
items.idea: Despite the AI-driven rally, the forward P/E of the S&P's top 10 stocks has dropped to the low end of its 10-year range — a function of earnings growing faster than price over the past few months.
items.angle: This directly complicates the 'AI bubble' narrative — multiple compression while prices hold near highs is what happens when growth outruns hype, not the reverse.
items.tweetA: The 'AI bubble' crowd should look at this: forward PE on the top 10 stocks is at the bottom of its 10-year range. Earnings are growing faster than the stocks are re-rating. That's the opposite of bubble math.
items.tweetB: Everyone quotes Mag7 market cap as the AI-bubble tell. Nobody quotes their forward multiples compressing to decade lows because it doesn't fit the narrative.

charts.desc: Top-10 stocks forward PE ratio, 10-year range chart (via @MikeZaccardi).

items.title: France just lost its 'core Europe' status — in the bond market, not politics
items.idea: French 10-year OAT yields are now trading above Spain's, Greece's, and near Italy's — a direct inversion of the post-crisis hierarchy where Germany and France sat as 'core' and everyone else was 'periphery.'
items.angle: This isn't a funding crisis — auctions are clearing fine — it's a re-rating of fiscal credibility that could turn into a much bigger story if it starts leaking into French bank credit or EUR volatility.
items.tweetA: France now pays more to borrow for 10 years than Spain. Not Italy — Spain. The core-vs-periphery map that's held since the euro crisis just got redrawn and almost nobody is pricing what that means for French bank credit.
items.tweetB: This isn't a France funding crisis, that's the wrong frame. It's a repricing of what 'core Europe' even means when Italy has more political stability than France walking into a 2027 election.

items.title: The real French risk isn't the OAT spread, it's what it spreads to
items.idea: French issuance is heavy and its maturity wall runs through 2027-28, colliding with higher rates and no ECB QE cushion — the danger is OAT widening transmitting into French bank credit, domestic equities, peripheral spreads, and EUR volatility.
items.angle: Watch French bank CDS and the OAT-Bund spread as the tripwire — if that starts moving together with peripheral spreads (Italy, Spain), it stops being a France story and becomes a eurozone story.
items.tweetA: France's 2027-28 maturity wall is arriving exactly when ECB QE isn't there to absorb it. If OAT stress starts showing up in French bank credit, this stops being a bond story and becomes a systemic one.
items.tweetB: The tell to watch isn't the OAT-Bund spread level, it's whether Italian and Spanish spreads start moving with France instead of independently. That's when a national repricing becomes contagion.

items.title: China's AI founders all trace back to one Tsinghua professor
items.idea: Z.ai's Tang Jie taught Moonshot AI's Yang Zhilin at Tsinghua; DeepSeek's Liang Wenfeng crossed paths with Tang in 2023. Nearly half of all Chinese equity-capital investment went into AI in H1 2026, and Beijing alone hosts 19 of China's top 50 AI companies.
items.angle: The US spent decades exporting its founder mythology (Gates and Jobs biographies) to Chinese engineers who studied it reverently — what's compounding back now isn't a copied playbook, it's a talent flywheel running under chip constraints the US doesn't have.
items.tweetA: Three of China's most important AI founders trace back to one Tsinghua professor's lab. That's not a coincidence, that's a flywheel: elite classes, open-source culture, teacher-to-student capital formation running at full speed.
items.tweetB: The US spent 40 years exporting Steve Jobs biographies to China. What compounds back from that isn't espionage-shaped. It's founder-education-shaped, and it's now running on a fifth of the chips US labs get.

charts.desc: Running scoreboard chart of China's top AI founders/companies, updated from ARD #127.

items.title: Anthropic's revenue run rate is now 65x Z.ai's — and Z.ai still went public first
items.idea: Z.ai's annualized revenue hit roughly $1B by July, about 2x DeepSeek's, and GLM-5.3 claims cybersecurity parity with Anthropic's Mythos 5 model. Meanwhile Anthropic's annualized revenue reached $65B in July.
items.angle: The capability gap between the leading US and Chinese labs (claimed parity on a cybersecurity benchmark) is much narrower than the revenue gap — which tells you the constraint right now is monetization and distribution, not model quality.
items.tweetA: Z.ai claims GLM-5.3 matches Anthropic's Mythos 5 on cybersecurity capability. Anthropic's revenue run rate is 65x Z.ai's anyway. The AI race isn't being decided on capability parity, it's being decided on who can actually sell it.
items.tweetB: DeepSeek's Liang was asked in May if he's worried about giving away his methods. His answer: the market is big enough, and the real gap is chips, not people. That's a founder who's already conceded the monetization race and is playing a different game.

items.title: Chinese AI labs get a fifth of the chips — and that constraint built the industry's best efficiency tricks
items.idea: Researchers at top Chinese labs say they're allotted roughly a fifth of the high-end chips available to OpenAI/Google peers, and Jefferies estimates Chinese tech firms invested under a fifth of what US counterparts did. That scarcity produced DeepSeek's multihead latent attention and early mixture-of-experts bets, which now run through Moonshot's K2/K3 too.
items.angle: Export controls successfully constrained chip supply; they didn't constrain the innovation response to that constraint — those efficiency techniques could eventually pressure global compute economics, including for US labs that adopt similar tricks.
items.tweetA: Export controls gave Chinese labs a fifth of the chips. The response wasn't slower AI, it was DeepSeek's memory-efficient attention mechanism that the whole Chinese industry copied within months. Constraint didn't stop the flywheel, it fed it.
items.tweetB: A fifth of the chips, under a fifth of the capex, and still shipping models that claim parity on real benchmarks. If you're modeling US AI capex as a moat, you're not accounting for the possibility the moat gets crossed on foot.

items.title: Unitree's Shanghai IPO closed up 460% this week, ~$50B valuation
items.idea: Unitree Robotics, founded by a DJI alum, closed its Shanghai debut up 460% this week, giving it a roughly $50 billion valuation — the hardware chapter of China's AI talent story landing in the same week as the Tsinghua-academic narrative.
items.angle: A 460% first-week pop is either extreme retail euphoria or a market pricing in China's humanoid robotics push catching up to the AI model story — worth checking whether this is a one-off or the start of a robotics IPO wave out of China.
items.tweetA: 460% pop, $50B valuation, first week of trading. Unitree just showed what happens when China's AI story finally gets a hardware chapter. Watch for copycat robotics IPOs out of Shanghai and Shenzhen next.
items.tweetB: Everyone's been trading the Chinese AI model story through Alibaba and Z.ai comps. Unitree just told you the humanoid robotics leg of that story is about to get its own valuation bubble, separate from the LLM one.

charts.desc: No chart in this section — referenced from ARD #145 coverage.

items.title: Gold's next leg may come from the options desk, not the Fed
items.idea: Treasury's long-end buyback announcement weakened the dollar far more than it moved yields, and gold has rallied roughly 15% off its July low toward $4,600/oz as Fed tightening fears fade — setting up a self-reinforcing options dynamic.
items.angle: This reframes gold as a fiscal-credibility hedge rather than a pure rates trade — if Treasury is willing to lean on the long end while the deficit keeps deteriorating, gold and dollar weakness become where that pressure gets expressed.
items.tweetA: Treasury announced bigger bond buybacks. Yields moved a little. The dollar cratered and gold jumped instantly. That's the market telling you exactly where the pressure from a $40T debt stock goes when policymakers lean on the long end: the currency.
items.tweetB: Gold at $4,600 isn't a rates story anymore. It's a bet that Washington will keep intervening in its own bond market, and every intervention pushes the adjustment into the dollar instead of yields.

items.title: 65,700 gold calls are stacked at $4,700-$5,000 — a gamma bomb waiting to go off
items.idea: CME data shows roughly 65,700 gold calls concentrated at the $4,700/$4,800/$4,900/$5,000 strikes through December expiries (about 6.6M oz of exposure), with over 22,000 calls alone at the $5,000 strike — if dealers are net short those calls, a push through $4,700 could force mechanical hedging buying that accelerates the rally.
items.angle: This is the mechanism, not just the direction — if gold gets momentum into $4,700, the options market itself becomes the accelerant rather than a brake, meaning the path to $5,000 could be faster and sharper than a purely fundamental story implies.
items.tweetA: 22,000+ gold calls stacked right at the $5,000 strike. If dealers are short those, gold breaking $4,700 doesn't just rally on fundamentals, it rallies because dealers are forced to chase the futures market higher to stay hedged. That's a mechanical accelerant, not a forecast.
items.tweetB: Everyone's fundamental case for $5,000 gold assumes central bank buying and ETF inflows. Nobody's pricing that the options market itself could be the thing that gets it there faster — or unwinds it faster if Fed-hike odds come back.

charts.desc: COMEX gold call open interest by strike ($4,700-$5,000), Sep-Dec expiries.

items.title: The 'copper wall' hits at 400G/lane — real, but further out than the hype suggests
items.idea: Copper interconnect still dominates within-rack at 200G/lane, but doubling lane speed halves copper's reach — at 400G/lane, intra-rack copper stops working, forcing a shift to integrated optics (CPO/NPO). That transition is at least two years out, in the 3.2T networking era.
items.angle: The optics-replaces-copper narrative gets ahead of the actual timeline — copper has a longer runway than bulls in the optics supply chain want you to think, which matters for how you time exposure to CPO/optics names versus copper interconnect suppliers.
items.tweetA: The optics bulls want you to think copper is dead now. It's not — copper wins within-rack through the 200G/lane generation, and the real 'copper wall' at 400G/lane is still 2+ years out. Timing matters more than direction here.
items.tweetB: Every lane-speed doubling halves copper's reach. That's the actual physics driving the copper-to-optics transition, and it means the winners in CPO/NPO get phased in by generation, not all at once.

items.title: Cutting HBM specs to save cost triples the networking bill
items.idea: If Nvidia's Rubin Ultra NVL572 de-specs from 12-hi HBM4E to 8-hi HBM4, memory's share of the rack bill-of-materials drops from 41% to 28% — but scale-up networking's share jumps from 4% to 12%, because fewer memory-per-rack forces more racks and more interconnect.
items.angle: This is a direct read-through for who benefits if hyperscalers cost-engineer around expensive memory: less spend flows to memory suppliers, more flows to networking/interconnect vendors — a rotation trade hiding inside a cost-cutting decision.
items.tweetA: If hyperscalers de-spec HBM to save money, memory's share of the rack bill drops from 41% to 28%. But networking's share triples, from 4% to 12%. Cost-cutting on memory doesn't save money, it just reroutes the spend to networking silicon.
items.tweetB: Nobody frames memory shortages as bullish for networking stocks, but that's exactly the mechanism: despec the HBM, add more racks, and the interconnect bill goes up 3x as a share of spend.

charts.desc: Rack BoM share chart: memory 41% to 28% vs scale-up networking 4% to 12% under the HBM de-spec scenario.

items.title: 800V is now the industry consensus for AI datacenter power
items.idea: Microsoft, Nvidia, Google, AMD and ASE all confirmed 800V/LVDC power architecture as the near-term standard at OCP APAC, with solid-state transformers positioned as the true end-game but not expected before 2030.
items.angle: This is a slow-moving but broad-based infrastructure consensus — worth tracking which power semiconductor and cooling suppliers are positioned for the 800V transition now versus the SST wave that's still years out.
items.tweetA: Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and AMD all confirmed the same thing this week: 800V is the new AI datacenter power standard. When that many hyperscalers converge on one spec, the supply chain behind it becomes the trade, not any single chip name.
items.tweetB: Solid-state transformers are the 'real' end-game for AI power delivery, and they're still years out, past 2030. The 800V rollout happening now is the bridge trade, not the destination.

items.title: Hartnett: Bessent's 3-3-3 plan is 0-for-3, and the debt clock hit $40T anyway
items.idea: BofA's Hartnett marks Bessent's original 3-3-3 framework (3% growth, 3% deficit, +3mbpd oil) to market: growth is running below target, the deficit is near double the goal, and oil production is a fraction of the promised increase — while total US debt has crossed $40 trillion.
items.angle: The market gave the administration a grace period to hit these targets; the props under equities and gold now increasingly depend on whether 'policy support' can keep bending long-end yields even as the underlying scorecard misses.
items.tweetA: Bessent's own 3-3-3 framework — 3% growth, 3% deficit, +3mbpd oil — is 0 for 3 according to Hartnett. And debt still crossed $40T anyway. The market's been pricing the promise, not the scorecard, and that gap is starting to matter.
items.tweetB: Forget the framework's original goals for a second. The fact that debt hit $40T with growth below target and the deficit near double target is the actual story — the arithmetic that was supposed to fix itself didn't.

items.title: Hartnett's three 'Maginot Lines': $4 gas, 160 USD/JPY, 5% long bond
items.idea: Hartnett frames gasoline above $4, USD/JPY around 160, and 5% long-bond yields as linked tripwires connecting energy, FX, Japanese capital flows, the dollar, and Treasury financing into a single policy problem — with the underlying question being whether the 'policy put' that's worked since QE1 still holds.
items.angle: These three levels function as a real-time scoreboard for policy credibility — watching all three simultaneously, not any one in isolation, is the actual signal for whether markets start questioning central bank and Treasury omnipotence.
items.tweetA: $4 gas, 160 yen, 5% long bond. Hartnett's three tripwires aren't separate stories, they're one story: whether the 'policymakers can always fix this' assumption that's held since QE1 still works. Watch all three together, not any one alone.
items.tweetB: 'Success is expected, failure is unthinkable' is Hartnett's way of saying the market has zero pricing for policy failure right now. That's the actual risk, not any single data point.

items.title: 30-year Treasury yield hit 5.327% — highest since 2007 — before Treasury's buyback rescue partially reversed
items.idea: The 30-year hit 5.327% last week, highest since 2007, on the combination of $40T federal debt, persistent inflation, and AI capex competing for capital. Treasury doubled its long-duration buyback size to $4B, yields fell initially, but by Friday most of that decline had already reversed to around 5.25%.
items.angle: The buyback 'rescue' barely worked and the yield mostly round-tripped within a week — that's a much weaker policy put than the initial market reaction suggested, and it's the key thing to watch heading into this week's 20-year auction.
items.tweetA: Treasury doubled its bond buybacks. Yields fell for a few hours, then round-tripped almost all the way back by Friday. If that's the policy put in action, it's a much weaker put than the initial rally implied.
items.tweetB: 5.327% on the 30-year, highest since 2007, in a week where AI capex is now explicitly competing with the US government for capital. That's the actual story under the Nvidia headlines this week.

items.title: Oil flow through Hormuz has collapsed from 20mbpd to 8mbpd — and only 4 ships crossed on Thursday
items.idea: Reuters reported the 7-day average flow through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen to roughly 8 million barrels per day from more than 20 million before the war; only four commodity ships transited on Thursday, none of them large crude or LNG carriers, while Iran selectively grants passage to Iraqi tankers.
items.angle: This is a live, ongoing 60%+ supply disruption through one of the world's most important chokepoints that isn't showing up as a headline oil price spike yet — the selective Iraqi tanker passage is the key tell on Iran's actual strategy: leverage, not full blockade.
items.tweetA: Oil flow through Hormuz is down 60% from pre-war levels — 8mbpd versus 20mbpd+ — and it's barely making headlines because oil prices haven't spiked to match. Someone is wrong here: either the disruption isn't as real as the flow data says, or the price hasn't caught up yet.
items.tweetB: Iran letting Iraqi tankers through while blocking almost everyone else isn't a blockade, it's a valve. That selectivity is the actual signal on Tehran's strategy — controlled pressure, not open war — and it's a very different trade than a full Hormuz closure.

charts.desc: No chart in this section — flow data cited from Reuters.

items.title: Nvidia's biggest customers told to expect 15%+ price hikes on AI servers due to memory costs
items.idea: Bloomberg/Reuters reported some of Nvidia's largest customers have been told server prices for systems with Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell chips could rise more than 15% due to surging memory costs, for systems shipping early next year; Nvidia hasn't confirmed the report.
items.angle: For two years the AI question was whether companies are spending enough. This flips it: is AI infrastructure now expensive enough to start eating into the economics of the hyperscalers doing the spending — right before Wednesday's Nvidia earnings, where investors need confirmation the buildout math still works.
items.tweetA: Nvidia's own customers are being told to expect 15%+ price hikes because of memory costs — two days before Nvidia reports earnings. The AI capex question just flipped from 'is anyone spending enough' to 'is the spend still economical.'
items.tweetB: Memory prices up, foundry prices up, power expensive, financing costs up — Broadcom alone reportedly exploring $60B+ in new financing. The AI buildout bottleneck isn't chips anymore, it's capital itself.

charts.desc: No chart — text reporting citing Bloomberg/Reuters.

items.title: US-Canada trade truce collapsed over the weekend — 50% tariffs on $20B of goods
items.idea: The US imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods (just over 5% of Canada's US exports) after negotiations broke down; Carney suspended talks, and Canada's retaliation begins September 8, targeting steel, electronics, dairy, and appliances.
items.angle: The direct macro hit is small, but the political rupture between two economies whose supply chains were assumed inseparable is the bigger tell — watch whether this becomes a template for how 'friendly' trade relationships get renegotiated under this administration.
items.tweetA: 50% tariffs, trade talks suspended, retaliation dated for September 8. Between the US and Canada — the relationship every trade model assumed was unbreakable. The macro hit is small (5% of Canada's exports), the precedent isn't.
items.tweetB: If the US will blow up a trade truce with its most integrated neighbor over a weekend, that's useful information for pricing every other 'stable' trade relationship on the board, not just Canada.

items.title: OAT-Bund spread hit 85.7bps Friday — widest since January 2025
items.idea: French 10-year yields have risen above both Spain and Italy; the OAT-Bund spread reached roughly 85.7 basis points Friday, its widest since January 2025, French 5-year CDS hit its highest level since late March, and a government-commissioned report warns debt could exceed 130% of GDP by 2030 without adjustment.
items.angle: Different specifics than the standalone France piece (exact 85.7bps level, CDS timing, the 130%-of-GDP warning) landing in the same morning's mail from the same desk — that repetition itself signals how much this has become the macro desk's top cross-asset worry.
items.tweetA: 85.7bps. That's how wide the OAT-Bund spread got Friday — widest since January 2025 — with a government report warning French debt could hit 130% of GDP by 2030. Two separate pieces from the same author landed on France this morning. That's not a coincidence, that's where the desk's attention is.
items.tweetB: Italy has 'baggage.' France currently can't manufacture the one thing Italy has: political stability. That inversion is what a 130%-of-GDP debt warning looks like when it's not even the scariest number in the piece.

items.title: Markets price 35% odds of a September hike, two-thirds by December — Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech is Friday
items.idea: After July's meeting produced three dissents, futures ended last week pricing roughly a 35% probability of a September hike and about two-thirds by December; new Fed chair Kevin Warsh gives his first Jackson Hole keynote Friday, August 28, having deliberately avoided heavy forward guidance.
items.angle: The real question isn't 25bps one way or the other — it's whether Warsh addresses where Fed policy ends and Treasury's long-end buyback intervention begins, since that boundary is what's actually driving cross-asset moves right now.
items.tweetA: Two-thirds odds of a Fed hike by December, and it's Treasury — not the Fed — that's been the one actively intervening in yields via buybacks. Kevin Warsh's Friday speech needs to address that overlap directly or the market will price the ambiguity itself.
items.tweetB: Three dissents at the last Fed meeting and a new chair who's deliberately withholding forward guidance. That's a Fed that wants markets to do the work of pricing data itself — exactly the kind of environment where vol tends to spike.

charts.desc: No chart — text reporting citing Reuters Wall Street Week Ahead.

items.title: Core PCE still running 3.3% in June — well above target — right as oil climbs back to the mid-$90s
items.idea: Core PCE was 3.3% year-on-year as of June, comfortably above the Fed's 2% target, with oil back toward the mid-$90s/bbl and tariffs still feeding into the inflation equation — all landing the same week as Wednesday's PCE release, GDP's second estimate, and Nvidia earnings.
items.angle: Three separate inflationary inputs — sticky core PCE, rising oil, fresh tariffs — are stacking into the same data window that determines whether Warsh's Fed leans hawkish: a genuinely loaded macro stress test, not just an Nvidia trade.
items.tweetA: 3.3% core PCE, oil back to the mid-$90s, and fresh 50% tariffs on Canada all landing in the same data window as Wednesday's PCE release. If you're only trading this week for the Nvidia number, you're missing three separate reasons the Fed could turn more hawkish than priced.
items.tweetB: Sticky inflation plus rising oil plus new tariffs is the textbook setup for a Fed that can't cut even if it wants to. Warsh inherits that setup for his very first Jackson Hole speech.

items.title: Multi-agent AI groups get the hidden-profile problem right only 17-36% of the time
items.idea: Anthropic ran a classic hidden-profile experiment on 4-agent groups, where only one agent holds the facts pointing to the correct answer: most model families got it right in just 17-36% of runs after group discussion, versus near-100% for a single agent given the full evidence. One model, Mythos 5, was an outlier at roughly 85%.
items.angle: This directly undercuts the 'just add more agents' scaling thesis for multi-agent systems — if agent swarms can't out-argue groupthink any better than humans can, the actual bottleneck for agentic AI value isn't more agents, it's giving individual agents better evidence and trusting them over consensus.
items.tweetA: Four AI agents given a decision where only one holds the correct evidence get it right 17-36% of the time after 'discussing' it. One agent alone, given all the evidence, gets it right almost 100% of the time. Multi-agent AI has the exact same groupthink problem as human committees.
items.tweetB: Mythos 5 hit roughly 85% on the hidden-profile test where every other model family cratered to 17-36%. Nobody knows why yet, but that's a much more interesting AI benchmark than another coding leaderboard — it's testing whether a model trusts a lone dissenting fact over consensus.

items.title: AI spend per employee: top 1% of firms up $6,542 since Oct 2023, the median firm up $9.63
items.idea: Exponential View's State of AI report found a 10% token price cut lifts usage only 12-18% — a weak Jevons paradox so far — and separately, since October 2023 the top 1% of firms by AI adoption raised AI spend per employee by $6,542 while the median firm raised it by just $9.63.
items.angle: That dispersion is the real story, not the muted price elasticity — a tiny slice of firms, mostly software where output is directly measurable via commits and pull requests, have figured out how to price a unit of AI work, while nearly everyone else hasn't started, meaning the AI-adoption S-curve is far earlier than aggregate spend numbers suggest.
items.tweetA: Top 1% of firms: +$6,542 AI spend per employee since Oct 2023. Median firm: +$9.63. That thousand-fold gap is the actual AI adoption story, not the aggregate spend number everyone quotes. Almost nobody outside software has actually started.
items.tweetB: Jevons paradox isn't failing to show up in AI, it's waiting on someone to figure out how to price a unit of knowledge work the way software already prices a commit. Until then, cheaper tokens just sit unused inside firms that can't turn them into billable output.

items.title: '$4M is the new $1M' — and the math behind it is uglier than the headline
items.idea: $50K at 5% in 1990 bought 66.75 S&P 500 shares; $200K at 5% today (the income off $4M) buys only about 26 units of the same index — meaning a 4x'd nominal wealth target still buys less purchasing power than the old $1M target did, once two decades of roughly 3.5% inflation are applied.
items.angle: This is a cleaner articulation of real-terms wealth-target inflation than most personal-finance math, and it has a direct market implication: high earners who run this arithmetic rationally shift from safe compounding toward business ownership and asymmetric risk-taking, which is a structural tailwind for risk-asset and private-market demand from a demographic that used to just index and chill.
items.tweetA: $50K bought 66.75 S&P shares in 1990. The equivalent income today ($200K off $4M) buys about 26 shares of the same index. 'The first $4M is the hardest' isn't a flex, it's what wealth-target inflation actually looks like in units of purchasing power, not dollars.
items.tweetB: Every high earner who runs this math ends up in the same place: safe compounding alone doesn't get you there anymore, so you take asymmetric risk instead. That's not a personal finance trend, that's a structural bid under every risky asset class this demographic touches.
